data.name: CLANNAD
data.detailed_description:
Story

After the death of his mother, Tomoya Okazaki—a guarded delinquent student at Hikarizaka High School—struggles to not only make sense of the abusive relationship he has with his alcoholic father, but also find meaning in his life. While on his way to class one morning, he meets a mystifying girl named Nagisa. She is a delinquent like him, but only because she is repeating her senior year, unlike the perpetually tardy Okazaki. From their brief encounter, Nagisa decides they should be friends, and enlists Tomoya's help to revive the school drama club. Not being busy in any way, he decides to join in. Along the way, the two make friends with many other students and try to find both solace and belonging in their endeavors.

New Features

HD Upgrade
All visuals have been upgraded to 1280x960 for the Steam release of CLANNAD.

Dangopedia
Exclusive to the English version of CLANNAD is the term encyclopedia, Dangopedia! It's a handy reference tool for understanding aspects of Japanese tradition and pop culture.

Achievements
Steam achievements are supported! There's also an in-game menu to review your progress.

reviews.review:
[h1]My personal essay on Clannad[/h1]

I've never been more indulgent with a game, or consistently made as much time for one as I have with Clannad. This game has changed me in ways I'm still trying to understand, it really has. I've made time to sit down and play it every day, and I only mention this because I've been wanting to make my life a busier one. In a way, I think this game has motivated me to make more room for fun in my life too.

For me, so far, Clannad is about two seniors mutually missing out on the fun of life. Tomoya has little regard for the world around him, largely because he's lost his sense of purpose. His mother died when he was young, leaving his father to fall into a deep depression. After his father attacked him under the influence, Tomoya suffered a shoulder injury that put an end to his basketball career. His father subsequently withdrew from him emotionally, using his own escapism to distance himself from his son. Tomoya describes him as practically a stranger. With his family life fractured and the future he once had taken away from him, it's understandable that he's become so apathetic toward the world.

Despite his apparent indifference, Tomoya repeatedly has moments of helping others pursue things that matter to them, without having figured out what it means for himself. What's interesting is the contrast between his willingness to involve himself in other people's lives and his apparent lack of investment in his own. Maybe I've actually overlooked the significance of this behavior, but it gives me more to wonder about.

Then there's Nagisa Furukawa, a tender girl whose illness kept her hospitalized for months, long enough for her graduating class to move on without her. Now she's back at school, with the people she once knew gone and the life she hoped to return to seemingly out of reach. She's left to start over, with little to hold on to besides the things she loves and the hopes she still wants to pursue. Tomoya helps her regain those things, whether it's her aspiration to revive the drama club or the smaller joys that give her something to look forward to. So her story feels like an attempt to reclaim the life that passed her by, while his feels like an attempt to find a reason to participate in life again.

I think that's what makes their stories work so well together. Both characters have become disconnected from the lives they could have been living, albeit for different reasons. They're still moving through their senior years, watching time pass, but neither seems to be experiencing the kind of youth they're supposed to be having. And as they begin to involve themselves in each other's lives, there's that possibility of change. I keep wondering how much of life they've missed out on, and how much they might still have left to experience...

That same idea extends to the other characters too. That they're all meandering through their own little worlds, or even through everyone else's, watching life go by as they try to find their place in it. I like how the game allows these individual lives to intersect and gives each character something worth caring about.

So far, I've finished Fuko Ibuki's route, and I was emotional for the entire second half of her story. I genuinely didn't know what to do with myself. Everything seemed to be going downhill, and I thought the game had suddenly become unforgiving and heartless! I felt like a fool for expecting everything to end on a sappy, happy note. I won't say much more about the route, but the experience left a real impression on me that was both really traumatizing and really funny, HAHA. Fuko is unbearably the cutest.

I went into this game with Furukawa as my end goal, and she will be. But I was so certain that she was the character I wanted to see the most of, and I wondered why anyone else could possibly change my mind. HAH! The writers proved me wrong. They managed to make me reconsider, to become invested in someone else's story, and to care about a character I hadn't expected to affect me so deeply. It's marvelous how well the writing adapts to each character, giving their stories enough weight to stand on their own. That's just character-driven writing for you though. That absence of traditional gameplay gives the characters and their stories room to take center stage. And with Clannad, that focus feels less like a limitation than a deliberate strength

You could say that I'm already attached to this game in a way that makes it difficult to put into words. It's immersive, yes, these things are probably typical of a visual novel. It has also just touched something in me that makes it difficult to look at it critically. I want to articulate all the interpretations and feelings I've been gathering as I play, but I think I need to sit with them for a while longer. Personally I think the pacing is great where it's at. It's a labor of love, in a way, because it naturally makes the characters feel like people you spend time with. You won't regret the time you spend on the filler portions of the story, it's much like taking a breather after a serious or decisive moment between you and the girls, rewarding the way I see it! There's so much I want to say, and I'm not even close to finishing.

I haven't watched the anime adaptation yet, but I definitely intend to. For now, I'll be making another review after I've experienced the remaining girls' routes, and eventually, I'll write one for Furukawa herself. I can't wait to see what else this game has loaded.

Thank you, Jun Maeda. Thank you, Key. And thank you to everyone else who worked on it.

11/10 FYTB.
